blocks.text: Design an object storage system like Amazon S3, durably storing an enormous, ever-growing volume of immutable objects, from tiny files to multi-terabyte uploads, while surviving individual disk and rack failures without ever actually losing customer data. This project's existing distributed cache and key-value store designs both accept losing a little data under extreme failure as a tolerable trade for speed. Object storage cannot make that trade at all, durability here is close to absolute, and achieving it cheaply, without paying the storage cost of keeping three or more full copies of everything, is the actual hard problem.

blocks.alt: An uploaded object is erasure encoded into data and parity shards distributed across separate disks, and losing any single disk still allows the missing shard to be reconstructed from the rest

blocks.text: The technique that makes this both durable and storage-efficient is erasure coding, splitting an object into several data shards plus a parity shard spread across physically separate disks, so that losing any single shard still allows it to be reconstructed exactly from the remaining ones, at a fraction of the storage overhead full replication would require.

blocks.text: A client should be able to upload an object, including very large ones split into multiple independently-uploaded parts, and have it committed atomically only once every part is confirmed. A client should be able to read back an object's exact, correct data at any time. The system should survive losing an individual disk, or even an entire rack, without losing any object stored on it. Access to an object or an entire bucket should be controlled per requester, and data should be encrypted at rest.

blocks.alt: Extremely durable and cheap, massive and ever-growing storage volume, reliable upload of very large objects, simple immutable versioning, and access-controlled, encrypted storage

blocks.text: Extremely durable, cheaply means losing a disk, or even an entire rack, must never mean losing real customer data, while still avoiding the cost of storing three or more full copies of everything. Massive, ever-growing storage volume means total storage only ever grows, reaching exabytes across an enormous number of individual objects. Reliable upload of very large objects means a multi-gigabyte or larger upload has to survive a partial failure without needing to restart from the very beginning. Simple, immutable versioning means an update to an object is really a new version, not a risky mutation of existing, already-durable data. And access-controlled, encrypted storage means every object and bucket has its own enforced permissions, with data encrypted at rest regardless.

blocks.text: This design implements and verifies a simple, real erasure coding scheme, data shards plus a single XOR-based parity shard, tolerating exactly one shard loss, the same underlying idea as RAID 5, rather than a more elaborate scheme tolerating multiple simultaneous losses. Multipart upload is assumed in scope, since reliably uploading very large objects is one of this design's genuine hard requirements. Objects are assumed immutable once committed, an update always creates a new version rather than mutating existing, already-durable shards in place.

Objects are assumed immutable once committed, an update always creates a new version rather than mutating existing, already-durable shards in place.

blocks.text: A platform at real scale might store trillions of objects, ranging from a few bytes to many terabytes each. Erasure coding needs roughly one and a half times the raw data size in total storage, data shards plus one parity shard, compared to three times the raw size for full triple replication, a significant, real cost saving at this volume. The system is designed to tolerate losing an entire disk, or even a whole rack, without losing any object stored across it.

blocks.text: An uploaded object, potentially assembled from several independently uploaded parts, is erasure encoded into data and parity shards, which are distributed across physically separate disks and racks for real fault isolation. Object metadata is stored separately, in its own fast, small lookup store, while a background reconstruction service continuously watches for lost shards and rebuilds them from the survivors.

blocks.alt: An object is assembled from its uploaded parts, erasure encoded into shards distributed across separate disks, with metadata stored separately and a background service reconstructing any lost shard

blocks.text: An object's data is split into several equal-sized data shards, and a parity shard is computed from all of them together. Every shard, data and parity alike, is stored on a physically separate disk, so that losing any single one of them still leaves enough information to recover it completely.

blocks.alt: An object is split into data shards plus a parity shard computed from them, with every shard stored on its own physically separate disk

blocks.text: If one shard's disk is lost, every other shard, whether data or parity, is still fully intact, and combining them together reconstructs exactly the missing shard's original content, restoring full readability with no actual data loss at all.

blocks.text: Object metadata is stored entirely separately from shard data, since metadata lookups are small, frequent, and latency-sensitive, while shard data is large, comparatively infrequently read in full, and physically distributed. Objects are versioned rather than mutated in place, an update always creates a new object version with its own fresh set of shards, keeping the durability guarantee simple, every committed version's shards are immutable from the moment they are written.

blocks.alt: An object, possibly uploaded in parts, is erasure encoded once complete, its shards distributed across separate disks, and its metadata committed
A routine integrity check finds a lost shard, and the reconstruction service rebuilds it from the remaining shards and stores it on a healthy disk

blocks.text: The happy path is the upload flow above, a complete object cleanly encoded and distributed across separate disks. The workflow worth walking through separately is what happens after a disk actually fails, routine integrity checks discover a lost shard, the reconstruction service reads every one of that object's remaining shards, and rebuilds the missing one exactly, storing it on a different, healthy disk, all without the object itself ever actually becoming unreadable during that process.

blocks.alt: A frequently requested object's metadata is served from a cache; a first-time or expired lookup reads from the metadata store, then caches the result

blocks.text: Metadata caching is a natural, low-risk optimization given how much more often an object's metadata is looked up than its underlying shards actually change, since an object is immutable once committed.

blocks.alt: A completed multipart upload is queued for erasure encoding, processed by workers that distribute the resulting shards across separate disks

blocks.text: Queuing the encode-and-distribute step lets a client's upload request complete once every part is confirmed, without needing to wait synchronously on the full erasure encoding and shard placement process to finish.

blocks.alt: An object's data and parity shards are deliberately placed on physically separate disks, ideally in different racks, to maximize genuine fault isolation

blocks.text: Shard placement is not an ordinary load-balancing decision at all, it is a deliberate fault-isolation one, placing two shards of the same object on the same disk or rack would defeat the entire point of erasure coding if that one disk or rack were ever lost.

blocks.alt: Rising storage utilization or a growing reconstruction backlog triggers adding more storage nodes or reconstruction workers

blocks.text: Because storage volume only ever grows, scaling here is primarily about continuously adding raw storage capacity and reconstruction throughput, rather than the request-rate-driven scaling pattern most other designs in this project follow.

blocks.text: The shard store scales by adding more disks and racks, spreading an ever-growing object count's shards across an ever-growing fault domain. The metadata store scales separately, as a much smaller, faster, more heavily-replicated store optimized for lookups rather than raw capacity.

blocks.alt: A specific object version's own data is strongly consistent, read-after-write, since it is immutable once committed; an object's listing and metadata visibility across replicas is eventually consistent, a brief propagation delay is acceptable

blocks.text: Because an object version never changes once committed, strong read-after-write consistency for the data itself is actually straightforward to provide, the harder consistency question is only ever about metadata visibility, such as how quickly a newly uploaded object shows up in a bucket listing.

blocks.alt: A disk failure is detected by routine integrity checks, and the missing shard is reconstructed from the survivors and re-stored on a healthy disk, all without the object itself becoming unavailable

blocks.text: This continuous, proactive reconstruction is what keeps durability a standing guarantee rather than something only discovered to have failed at the moment a client happens to try reading an affected object, a lost shard is detected and repaired long before it would ever actually matter to a real read.

blocks.alt: A request to read or write an object is checked against that requester's permissions for the specific object or bucket; data is encrypted at rest regardless of the outcome

blocks.text: Access control and encryption at rest are this design's defining security concerns, distinct from every other category's angle in this project, since object storage is often the single most durable, longest-lived home for an organization's actual data, making a permissions mistake or an unencrypted disk a uniquely consequential failure mode.

blocks.text: Erasure coding is the right default at this scale because it delivers durability comparable to full replication at a fraction of the storage cost, and at the exabyte scale this design operates at, that difference in overhead is the difference between a viable and an unviable business.

Separating metadata from shard data avoids paying shard-store-level storage and access costs for the comparatively tiny, frequently-read metadata that does not actually need it.

items: A disk holding a data shard fails, correctly reconstructed from the remaining data and parity shards without any actual read ever failing.
A disk holding the parity shard itself fails, correctly leaving the object fully readable from its intact data shards alone, since parity is only needed for reconstruction, not ordinary reads.
One part of a multipart upload fails partway through, correctly requiring only that specific part to be retried rather than the entire upload restarting.

Two shards of the same object are lost simultaneously, correctly exceeding what a single parity shard can tolerate, an honest limitation this design's trade-off table addresses directly rather than silently ignoring.

blocks.text: A change to the erasure coding scheme itself, such as its data-to-parity shard ratio, needs extremely careful, gradual rollout, since it directly affects the platform's core durability guarantee for every object going forward. Reconstruction service changes deserve equal caution, a bug that fails to detect or correctly rebuild a lost shard silently erodes the exact guarantee this entire design exists to provide.

blocks.text: A more advanced erasure coding scheme, such as genuine Reed-Solomon coding rather than simple XOR parity, would tolerate multiple simultaneous shard losses rather than only one, at a correspondingly higher storage overhead. Tiered storage, automatically moving rarely-accessed objects to a cheaper, higher-latency storage class, would reduce cost for the long tail of infrequently-read data without touching this design's core durability guarantee.

items: Architecture: multipart-assembled objects erasure encoded into data and parity shards distributed across separate disks, with metadata stored separately and continuous background reconstruction.
Capacity: trillions of stored objects, roughly one and a half times raw data size in storage overhead versus three times for full replication, and tolerance for losing an entire disk or rack.
The core techniques: XOR-based erasure coding and shard reconstruction, both worked through with a real, verified implementation in Java, Python, and C++.
Database: a shard store partitioned across disks and racks for fault isolation, alongside a separate, fast metadata store.
End-to-end workflows: a normal upload-and-encode flow and a shard reconstruction flow, both traced as sequence diagrams.
Consistency: strongly consistent, immutable object data once committed, paired with an eventually consistent metadata listing view.
Trade-offs: erasure coding versus full triple replication versus no redundancy at all, compared directly on storage overhead and tolerated simultaneous losses.
